title: 'Sandford & Son' Star Redd Foxx Believed "It's Pretty Hard To Hate Someone Who Makes You Laugh" - NewsBreak
text:
8 hours ago Photo by commons.wikimedia.org It's been more than thirty years since the tragic demise of beloved comedian Redd Foxx . The star of the groundbreaking TV sitcom, Sanford and Son (NBC, 1972-1977), Foxx died of a heart attack on the set of last series, The Royal Family (CBS, 1991-1992). He was only 68 years old, his humor was edgy, and crossed all cultural lines, and united humanity in his own way.
Redd Foxx poses, and 'Sanford and Son' co-star Demond Wilson stands by, literally, in this 1972 publicity still for the classic sitcom. Photo by commons.wikimedia.org Backstory Redd Foxx was born John Elroy Sanford in St. Louis, Mo. When he was only 4 years old, his father deserted the family, which included his mother.
Foxx was kicked out of school for tossing a book at a teacher who had first tossed it at him. He quit high school after one year to form a washtub band with his two pals, Lamont Ousley and Steve Trimel.
In 1939, the red-headed Foxx sought fame and ran away from home. He eventually met and befriended the also-then-red-headed Malcolm Little. John Sanford became 'Chicago Red' and Little became 'Detroit Red' at the Harlem restaurant where they were employed as dishwashers.
Chicago Red later added an extra “d” to Red and changed his last name to Foxx, because he fancied himself a stylish dresser.
Little later changed his name to 'Malcolm X' and went on to make his own historical mark in the world. In his autobiography, X recalled Foxx as "the funniest dishwasher on this earth."
A "Foxxy" Move Following bawdy nightclub gigs in New York Redd Foxx moved to Hollywood in Hollywood in the 1950s and began recording his routines. By 1960, he was performing in Las Vegas, and in 1970 signed a three-year, $960,000 contract guaranteeing him 32 weeks a year in Las Vegas at $10,000 a week.
In 1969, Foxx was cast as a junk dealer in the movie Cotton Comes to Harlem , after which TV producers Bud Yorkin and Norman Lear signed him for Sanford and Son.
As with the duo's hit CBS series, All in the Family , Sanford and Son was adapted from a British TV show. Foxx then became a household name due to his portrayal of Fred G. Sanford on Sanford and Son .
In 1976, Redd Foxx left NBC to star in a failed ABC comedy-variety show. Three years later, Foxx reunited with NBC with a new Sanford sitcom, which also failed.
In 1989, Foxx starred with Eddie Murphy and Richard Pryor in the Harlem Nights feature film.
In 1991, Foxx was starred in The Royal Family Foxx, co-starring Della Reese (later of TV's Touched By An Angel ). He portrayed Al Royal, a retired Atlanta postman whose life changes when his adult daughter moves back home with her three children. For many viewers, however, the role was just a reprise as the cranky Fred G. Sanford, a name Foxx selected as a tribute to his brother who had died in 1968.
The Day He Died In his final years, Redd Foxx, once at the top of his game, faced economic and IRS issues. According to his official website , the day on the set of The Royal Family, co-star Della Reese bent over him and prayed, “Don’t die Redd...don’t die,” but it was too late. The world lost comedic genius Redd Foxx on October 11, 1991. Foxx’s albums stand as proof of his legacy as they continue to sell, topping out at over 15 million copies sold."
In the Big Picture According to the book, Tops in TV, by David Dachs, Redd Foxx once concluded, "We all have to do our own thing. Mine is to make people laugh. That is the best way I know how to bring us all together."
"It's pretty hard to hate someone who makes you laugh," he concluded. 112
